theory_mcq.question: In Kahn's algorithm, why does `result.length < n` indicate a cycle in the graph?
options: Shorter results mean some vertices were skipped due to memory limits

Kahn's algorithm only processes vertices whose IN-DEGREE REACHES ZERO — a vertex with all prerequisites done; in a CYCLE (e.g., A→B→C→A), each vertex in the cycle has at least one incoming edge that can never be satisfied (the predecessor in the cycle is never fully processed first); these vertices never reach in-degree 0, so they're never enqueued; if any vertex is never processed, result.length < n — directly revealing the cycle
result.length < n means there were disconnected components that were skipped
Kahn's algorithm counts edges not vertices; length < n is an unrelated condition
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Cycle detection: if result length < V, a cycle exists' — vertices in a cycle can never have their in-degree reach 0 because their circular predecessor always contributes an unresolved incoming edge; such vertices never enter the queue and are never appended to result; the count discrepancy precisely identifies cycle presence.

theory_mcq.question: What is the IN-DEGREE of a vertex, and why does Kahn's algorithm start by enqueueing all zero-in-degree vertices?
options: In-degree is the number of outgoing edges; zero-in-degree vertices have no successors

IN-DEGREE is the NUMBER OF INCOMING EDGES to a vertex — the number of other vertices that must precede it; zero-in-degree vertices have NO PREREQUISITES — nothing must come before them in the topological order; these are the natural STARTING POINTS of the ordering; enqueueing them first ensures we begin with safely-schedulable tasks and then progressively unlock their successors as each prerequisite is satisfied
In-degree is the depth level of a vertex in the BFS tree
Zero-in-degree vertices are always source nodes in the original problem domain
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'In-degree: number of incoming edges to a vertex' and 'Kahn's algorithm: start with all zero-in-degree vertices in a queue' — zero in-degree means no prerequisite constraints; these vertices can be validly placed first in any topological ordering; the algorithm then removes their outgoing edges (by decrementing successors' in-degrees), potentially creating new zero-in-degree vertices.

logic_mcq.question: For `topoSortKahn(4, [[0,1],[0,2],[1,3],[2,3]])`, what are the initial in-degrees and what is the first vertex dequeued?
options: inDegrees=[0,1,1,2]; vertex 0 is first dequeued — confirmed: 0 has no incoming edges; 1 and 2 each have one incoming from 0; 3 has two incoming from 1 and 2
inDegrees=[1,0,0,1]; vertices 1 and 2 are dequeued first
inDegrees=[0,0,0,0]; all vertices dequeued simultaneously
inDegrees=[2,1,1,0]; vertex 3 is dequeued first
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: inDegrees for edges [0→1,0→2,1→3,2→3]: inDegree[0]=0 (no incoming), inDegree[1]=1 (from 0), inDegree[2]=1 (from 0), inDegree[3]=2 (from 1 and 2); vertex 0 is the only zero-in-degree vertex and is enqueued first; after processing 0, vertices 1 and 2 both reach in-degree 0.

logic_mcq.question: After dequeuing vertex 0, what happens to the in-degrees of vertices 1 and 2, and which vertex is next dequeued (if any)?
options: inDeg[1] becomes 0 and inDeg[2] becomes 0; both are enqueued; either 1 or 2 is next

inDeg[1]-- → 0, enqueue 1; inDeg[2]-- → 0, enqueue 2; the queue now has [1,2]; vertex 1 is dequeued next (FIFO queue) giving result=[0,1]; then 2 is dequeued; after dequeuing 1, inDeg[3]-- → 1; after dequeuing 2, inDeg[3]-- → 0, enqueue 3
Only inDeg[1] changes; inDeg[2] requires a separate edge decrement
inDeg[1]=1, inDeg[2]=1 remain unchanged; vertex 0 had no effect
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution returning [0,1,2,3]; processing vertex 0's adjacency [1,2]: inDeg[1] decrements to 0 (enqueue), inDeg[2] decrements to 0 (enqueue); FIFO queue: next is vertex 1; after vertex 1, inDeg[3] becomes 1; after vertex 2, inDeg[3] becomes 0 (enqueue); final result [0,1,2,3].

syntax_mcq.question: In Kahn's algorithm, `queue.shift()` dequeues from the front (FIFO). What would happen if `queue.pop()` (LIFO) were used instead?
options: pop() and shift() produce identical topological orderings

Using `pop()` makes the queue behave as a STACK (LIFO), turning Kahn's BFS into a DFS-like traversal; the result is STILL a valid topological order (as long as the graph is a DAG), but it may differ from the BFS order produced by `shift()`; the important correctness property (u before v for every edge u→v) is preserved regardless of FIFO/LIFO; only the specific ordering among equally-valid alternatives changes
pop() would cause an infinite loop for DAGs
pop() produces a reverse topological order that must be reversed again
syntax_mcq.explanation: The choice of FIFO (shift/queue) vs LIFO (pop/stack) among zero-in-degree vertices doesn't affect correctness — any order of processing zero-in-degree vertices produces a valid topological sort; it only affects WHICH valid ordering is produced; for lexicographically smallest order, a sorted structure (min-heap) is used instead; the lesson notes `topoSortKahnLex` uses sort for this purpose.

theory_mcq.question: Why does DFS POST-ORDER reversed give the correct topological ordering?
options: Post-order is naturally sorted by vertex index

In DFS post-order, vertex u is appended to result AFTER all vertices reachable from u (all descendants) are fully processed; for any edge u→v: v is processed (appended) BEFORE u in post-order; REVERSING the post-order list puts u BEFORE v — exactly the topological constraint 'u before v'; this reversal transforms the natural DFS finishing time into the correct topological precedence
Post-order traversal visits leaves first, which happen to be topologically last
DFS post-order and pre-order produce identical topological orderings
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explanation: 'For edge u->v: v is processed (appended) BEFORE u. After reversal: u comes before v. Correct topological order' — post-order appends after descendants; reversal inverts this to match the 'predecessors before successors' requirement; this is the key insight behind DFS-based topological sort.

theory_mcq.question: What do the THREE STATES (0, 1, 2) represent in DFS topological sort, and which state signals a CYCLE?
options: 0=visited, 1=parent, 2=leaf; state 2 signals a cycle

State 0 = UNVISITED (not yet reached); State 1 = IN CURRENT DFS PATH (gray — currently being explored); State 2 = FULLY PROCESSED (black — completely done with all descendants); encountering STATE 1 signals a CYCLE: if we reach a vertex that is currently on the active DFS path (state 1), it means there's a back edge — we've looped back to a vertex in our own ancestry chain, forming a directed cycle
0=unvisited, 1=visited, 2=processed; state 0 signals a cycle
All three states are needed only for disconnected graphs; connected graphs use two states
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concepts: '0=unvisited, 1=in current DFS path, 2=fully processed' and 'Cycle detection: encountering a state-1 vertex = back edge = cycle' — the three-colour (white/gray/black) DFS is the standard algorithm for directed cycle detection; state-2 vertices can be safely skipped (already processed); state-1 indicates a back edge to an ancestor in the current DFS tree.

logic_mcq.question: Why is the outer loop `for (let v = 0; v < n; v++) if (state[v] === 0) dfs(v)` needed in DFS topological sort?
options: The outer loop is a redundancy check; it only activates when the graph has cycles

The outer loop handles DISCONNECTED COMPONENTS: in a DAG with disconnected subgraphs, a single DFS from vertex 0 might not reach all vertices (if 0 has no outgoing edges to some component); iterating over all unvisited vertices ensures every vertex is visited exactly once, including isolated vertices and vertices in separate weakly-connected components; this is identical to the pattern used in Number of Islands and other multi-component graph problems
The outer loop restarts DFS from scratch on each iteration
The outer loop is only needed when the graph is given as an edge list rather than adjacency list
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Handles disconnected components: run DFS from all unvisited vertices' — a single DFS may not reach all vertices in a disconnected DAG; the outer loop ensures completeness; the `state[v]===0` check prevents re-visiting already-processed vertices, so each vertex is DFS-explored exactly once.

logic_mcq.question: For the same graph [[0,1],[0,2],[1,3],[2,3]], Kahn's produces [0,1,2,3] while DFS produces [0,2,1,3] (different order). Are BOTH valid topological orderings?
options: Only one topological order is valid for any DAG

BOTH are valid — a topological sort is valid if for every directed edge u→v, u appears before v in the result; both [0,1,2,3] and [0,2,1,3] satisfy: 0 before 1 ✓, 0 before 2 ✓, 1 before 3 ✓, 2 before 3 ✓; there can be MULTIPLE valid topological orderings for a DAG (when some vertices have no relative ordering constraint); the different results reflect the different traversal strategies (BFS-FIFO vs DFS-recursion depth)
DFS always produces the same result as Kahn's for any DAG
[0,2,1,3] is invalid because 2 appears before 1 which is not allowed
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: Kahn's returns [0,1,2,3] and DFS returns [0,2,1,3]; both are valid since vertices 1 and 2 have no ordering constraint between them (neither has an edge to the other); any topological sort allows either ordering for unconstrained pairs; the lesson notes 'Both O(V+E) time O(V) space' with different result structures but equivalent correctness.

syntax_mcq.question: In the DFS topological sort, `state[u] = 2` and `result.push(u)` happen AFTER the neighbour loop. Why must these two lines come AFTER (not before) the recursion?
options: The order is arbitrary; JavaScript executes these lines simultaneously with the loop

Setting state[u]=2 and pushing u MUST happen AFTER all neighbours are recursed: if state[u] were set to 2 BEFORE recursing into v, then if v loops back to u, the check `state[v]===1` would not trigger (u is already 2); the cycle would be UNDETECTED; similarly, pushing u BEFORE its descendants would produce pre-order (not post-order), giving an INCORRECT topological ordering after reversal; both the cycle detection and the ordering correctness depend on post-order execution
Post-order is optional; pre-order works equally well for topological sort
state[u]=2 must come before result.push(u) for initialization purposes
syntax_mcq.explanation: The post-order placement (after recursion) is essential for both correctness invariants: (1) cycle detection requires state[u]=1 to remain active while u's subtree is explored; setting state[u]=2 early would miss back edges to u; (2) post-order placement ensures all descendants appear in result before u, so reversal correctly places u before its successors.

theory_mcq.question: In Course Schedule, prerequisite `[a, b]` means 'take b before a'. Why does this translate to edge b→a in the graph (not a→b)?
options: Edge direction is arbitrary; both directions produce the same result

A DIRECTED EDGE u→v in a topological sort means 'u must come before v'; if [a,b] means 'b before a', then the edge must be b→a (b precedes a); if we built edge a→b instead, topological sort would put a before b, which REVERSES the prerequisite — a would come first even though b must be taken first; the edge direction encodes the 'before' relationship: source → destination means 'source is scheduled before destination'
The edge direction doesn't matter for Kahn's algorithm
Edge a→b is correct; the lesson has an error in the implementation
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Edge direction: prerequisite→course (b→a for [a,b]) in the ordering' — topological sort outputs u before v for every edge u→v; to enforce 'b before a', the edge must be b→a; building edge a→b would output a before b, contradicting the prerequisite; `adj[b].push(a)` in the code correctly implements this.

Course Schedule II requires additional BFS passes to determine the exact order
Course Schedule I is O(V) while Course Schedule II is O(V+E) due to the extra tracking
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Course Schedule I: check result.length==n; Course Schedule II: return result or [] if impossible' — the Kahn's BFS is identical in both problems; the order array is built naturally as vertices are dequeued; Course Schedule I just checks if the count matches; Course Schedule II returns the order itself; this demonstrates how a single algorithm solves both variants with minimal code change.

logic_mcq.question: For `findOrder(4, [[1,0],[2,0],[3,1],[3,2]])`, what edges are built in the graph and what is the resulting order?

Edges 1→0, 2→0, 3→1, 3→2; result is reverse [3,2,1,0]
All four edges point from 3; result starts with 3
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution returning [0,1,2,3]; prerequisites [a,b] build edge b→a: [1,0]→0→1, [2,0]→0→2, [3,1]→1→3, [3,2]→2→3; course 0 has no prerequisites (in-degree=0) and is scheduled first; 1 and 2 depend only on 0; 3 depends on both 1 and 2.

The cycle is course 0 requiring course 1 and vice versa; canFinish returns true because 0+1=1
No cycle exists; both courses can be completed independently

syntax_mcq.question: In `findOrder`, `if (--inDeg[v] === 0) queue.push(v)` uses the pre-decrement `--inDeg[v]`. How does this differ from `inDeg[v]--; if (inDeg[v] === 0)`?
options: Both forms are identical in JavaScript

Both forms produce the SAME RESULT for this specific use case: pre-decrement `--inDeg[v]` decrements first then evaluates (reading the NEW value); post-decrement `inDeg[v]--; if (inDeg[v]===0)` decrements first (in the separate statement) then checks the new value; functionally equivalent here; the pre-decrement form is more CONCISE (single expression) and common in competitive programming; the lesson's `if (--inDeg[v] === 0)` is a stylistic choice for brevity
Pre-decrement mutates the array; post-decrement creates a copy
Pre-decrement is O(1); post-decrement requires array reallocation
syntax_mcq.explanation: In this specific context (decrement then check zero), both pre-decrement-in-condition and post-decrement-with-separate-check produce identical results: both decrement inDeg[v] and then check if the new value equals 0; pre-decrement is idiomatic shorthand; the lesson uses `--inDeg[v]` consistently as a compact form without semantic difference.

theory_mcq.question: In Alien Dictionary, why does only the FIRST DIFFERING CHARACTER between two adjacent words give an ordering rule?
options: All differing characters give ordering rules; only the first is implemented for efficiency

The alien words are LEXICOGRAPHICALLY SORTED in the alien alphabet; comparing adjacent words character by character: the FIRST POSITION where they differ reveals the relative ordering of those two characters in the alien alphabet; characters at LATER POSITIONS cannot be inferred — for example, if word1='ba' and word2='bc', we know b<b is not a rule (same); 'a' vs 'c' at position 1 tells us a comes before c; but characters after the first difference give no information (they might occur in any order in the alien alphabet); `break` after the first difference is NECESSARY for correctness
Only the last differing character is used; the first is arbitrary
All characters in both words contribute to the ordering rules
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'First differing character between adjacent words gives one ordering rule' and the code: `break; // only first differing char gives ordering info` — in a sorted list, adjacent entries share the longest common prefix; the relative order is determined entirely by the first position where they differ; subsequent characters could appear in any order in the alien alphabet and cannot be inferred.

theory_mcq.question: What INVALID INPUT condition does Alien Dictionary check for, and why does it immediately return ''?
options: Invalid input is when two identical words are adjacent

INVALID: `words[i]` is a PREFIX of `words[i+1]` but `words[i]` is LONGER — e.g., ['abc','ab'] where 'ab' comes after 'abc' which is impossible in any sorted order (shorter strings always precede their longer prefix in lexicographic order); detected by: `w1.length > w2.length && w1.slice(0, minLen) === w2`; this returns '' immediately because no valid alien alphabet can explain this ordering — it's an impossibility, not just a cycle
Invalid input is when any word contains non-alphabetic characters
Invalid input occurs when there are more than 26 unique characters
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concept: 'Invalid input: word[i] is a prefix of word[i+1] but comes after it' — in any sorted list, a string must precede all strings for which it is a proper prefix; if 'abc' appears before 'ab' in the word list, this is impossible regardless of character ordering; the code checks for this and returns '' (invalid/empty) before even attempting topological sort.

logic_mcq.question: For `alienOrder(['wrt','wrf','er','ett','rftt'])`, what ordering RULES are derived from adjacent word comparisons?
options: Rules: t→f (wrt vs wrf: position 2, 't' before 'f'); r→t (er vs ett: position 1, 'r' before 't'); e→r (ett vs rftt: position 0, 'e' before 'r'); w→e (wrt vs er: position 0, 'w' before 'e'); giving graph t<f, r<t, e<r, w<e → ordering w,e,r,t,f = 'wertf' — confirmed by direct execution
Only one rule is derived: 'w' before 'e'
Rules are derived from all character pairs, not just adjacent words
The rule set includes r→e and f→t which reverse the actual ordering
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution returning 'wertf'; rules: wrt vs wrf→t before f; er vs ett→r before t; ett vs rftt→e before r; wrt vs er→w before e; graph: w→e→r→t→f; topological sort gives w,e,r,t,f confirming all positional constraints.

logic_mcq.question: Why does `alienOrder(['z','x','z'])` return '' (empty string)?
options: The function returns '' because there are only 2 unique characters

Comparing 'z' and 'x': z→x (z comes before x). Comparing 'x' and 'z': x→z (x comes before z). This creates cycle z→x→z; topological sort finds a cycle (result.length < inDeg.size); returns '' indicating no valid alien alphabet exists — confirmed by direct execution returning empty string
The function returns '' because 'z' appears twice
The empty string is returned when all input words are single characters
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: 'z','x' → rule z→x; 'x','z' → rule x→z; these two rules form a cycle (z→x→z); Kahn's topological sort cannot process the cycle; result.length < inDeg.size → return ''; the cycle means no valid ordering of the alien alphabet satisfies both constraints simultaneously.

syntax_mcq.question: In `alienOrder`, the adjacency list uses `adj.set(c, new Set())` (a Set of neighbours) rather than an array. Why use a Set for the neighbour list?
options: Set is always faster than Array for adjacency lists

DEDUPLICATION: two different adjacent word pairs might derive the SAME ordering rule (e.g., 'ab' before 'ac' and 'ab' before 'ad' both tell us 'a' doesn't need additional edges from a); if the same edge c1→c2 is 'derived' from multiple word pair comparisons, storing in a Set automatically deduplicates; the code checks `if (!adj.get(w1[j]).has(w2[j]))` before adding — using a Set makes this both the membership check and the storage in one structure; without deduplication, in-degrees would be incorrectly inflated
Set prevents the `break` statement from terminating the wrong loop
Set is required because characters (not integers) are the keys
syntax_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `if (!adj.get(w1[j]).has(w2[j])) { adj.get(w1[j]).add(w2[j]); inDeg.set(w2[j], inDeg.get(w2[j])+1); }` — this guard prevents adding duplicate edges; a Set makes the `.has()` check O(1) and `.add()` idempotent; without deduplication, the same rule derived from multiple word pairs would increment in-degree multiple times, corrupting Kahn's algorithm.

theory_mcq.question: What is the difference between an EULERIAN PATH and a TOPOLOGICAL SORT? Why does Reconstruct Itinerary use a different algorithm?
options: Both solve the same problem; Hierholzer's is just a renamed topological sort

TOPOLOGICAL SORT: orders VERTICES such that all edges point forward (for dependency problems on DAGs); EULERIAN PATH: finds a path that visits every EDGE exactly once (not just vertices); Reconstruct Itinerary requires using each ticket (edge) exactly once — a classic Eulerian path problem; topological sort would only ensure vertex ordering; Hierholzer's algorithm specifically handles the 'visit each edge once' constraint via DFS with post-order reversal, which ensures dead-ends are placed correctly in the reverse itinerary
Eulerian path is for undirected graphs only; topological sort is for directed
Both algorithms use identical code; the difference is only in problem framing
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concepts: 'Eulerian path: path that visits every EDGE exactly once' and 'Topological sort: linear ordering of vertices where every edge u->v has u before v' — the fundamental difference: topo sort orders vertices; Eulerian path uses edges; Reconstruct Itinerary is an Eulerian path problem (use every ticket/edge once) requiring Hierholzer's algorithm, not topological sort.

theory_mcq.question: Why is POST-ORDER REVERSAL the key insight in Hierholzer's algorithm for Reconstruct Itinerary?
options: Post-order reversal is only needed when the graph has dead-end airports

Hierholzer's uses post-order because DEAD-ENDS (airports with no outgoing tickets) must appear LAST in the itinerary, but DFS visits them FIRST; when DFS reaches a dead-end, it has no more edges to follow — it appends the dead-end airport to result (post-order); when the dead-end is found early (e.g., a stub path), it should appear LATE in the itinerary (after all detours are taken); appending in post-order and then reversing naturally places early-dead-ends at the end of the reconstructed itinerary
Post-order is needed only to handle the starting airport JFK
The reversal converts DFS pre-order to topological order for the airports
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's trace: 'dfs(JFK) explores SFO which explores JFK which explores ATL which explores SFO (dead-end → appended first); ATL appended second; JFK appended; SFO appended; JFK appended last; reverse gives correct itinerary' — post-order naturally handles the case where a path stub must be 'saved' until after the main itinerary routes are exhausted.

logic_mcq.question: For tickets `[['MUC','LHR'],['JFK','MUC'],['SFO','SJC'],['LHR','SFO']]`, what is the reconstructed itinerary?
options: ['JFK','MUC','LHR','SFO','SJC'] — the only valid Eulerian path from JFK using all 4 tickets — confirmed by direct execution
['JFK','SFO','SJC','MUC','LHR'] — sorted by destination alphabetically
['JFK','LHR','MUC','SFO','SJC'] — incorrect ticket usage
There is no valid itinerary starting from JFK
logic_mcq.explanation: Confirmed by direct execution: ['JFK','MUC','LHR','SFO','SJC']; the only path from JFK that uses all 4 tickets: JFK→MUC (ticket 2), MUC→LHR (ticket 1), LHR→SFO (ticket 4), SFO→SJC (ticket 3); each airport has exactly the connections needed for this single valid Eulerian path.

logic_mcq.question: Why does the algorithm reverse the adjacency lists (using `dests.reverse()` before DFS) and then use `pop()` instead of `shift()`?
options: pop() is incorrect; shift() must always be used for correct ordering

After sorting destinations ASCENDING (lexicographic order) and then REVERSING them, the smallest destination is now at the END of the array; `pop()` removes from the END in O(1); this is more efficient than `shift()` which removes from the START in O(n) (requires shifting all elements); the reverse-then-pop pattern gives O(1) lexicographic-smallest extraction — a common trick when processing sorted arrays from front to back using a stack-like interface
pop() and shift() produce the same ordering regardless of sort direction
Reversing is needed only for airports with more than 3 outgoing tickets
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's comment: 'So reverse sort to use pop() instead of shift()' — `shift()` is O(n) because it removes from the front and shifts all elements; `pop()` is O(1) from the end; sorting ascending then reversing puts the smallest at the end, making `pop()` equivalent to taking the smallest destination; this optimization is common for priority-based greedy DFS.

syntax_mcq.question: In `findItinerary`, `const dests = adj.get(airport) || []` uses `|| []` as a fallback. When is this fallback needed?
options: The fallback is always triggered; adj.get always returns undefined

The fallback `|| []` handles airports that appear ONLY AS DESTINATIONS (never as origins) — these airports have no outgoing tickets and therefore no entry in the `adj` Map; when DFS visits such an airport, `adj.get(airport)` returns `undefined`; without `|| []`, iterating `undefined` with `while(dests.length)` would throw a TypeError; the `|| []` provides an empty array as a safe default, correctly representing 'no outgoing tickets from this airport' (it's a dead-end)
The fallback handles the case when adj has been garbage collected
|| [] converts the return type from Set to Array for the while loop
syntax_mcq.explanation: The `|| []` fallback handles dead-end airports: if an airport appears as a destination (in some ticket's 'to' field) but never as a source (no ticket departs from it), it's never added to adj; adj.get returns undefined for such airports; `|| []` safely converts this to an empty array, allowing the while loop to terminate immediately for dead-ends.

theory_mcq.question: What are the RECOGNITION SIGNALS that indicate Topological Sort vs Eulerian Path for a graph problem?
options: Both signals are interchangeable; any graph problem can use either algorithm

TOPOLOGICAL SORT SIGNALS: 'ordering', 'dependencies', 'valid schedule', 'DAG', 'what must come before what' — the problem involves VERTEX ORDERING respecting directed constraints; EULERIAN PATH SIGNALS: 'use every edge once', 'reconstruct itinerary', 'visit all connections', 'Euler circuit' — the problem involves traversing EVERY EDGE exactly once; the key distinction: topo sort is about VERTEX ORDERING in DAGs; Eulerian path is about EDGE COVERAGE in any directed graph
Topological sort applies to weighted graphs; Eulerian path to unweighted
Both algorithms apply only to undirected graphs
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's concepts: "Topological sort signals: 'ordering', 'dependencies', 'valid schedule', DAG required" and "Eulerian path signals: 'use every edge once', 'reconstruct itinerary', Hierholzer's" — the problem domain (vertex ordering vs edge traversal) is the primary distinguishing feature; recognizing this within 60 seconds is the target skill.

theory_mcq.question: In the COMPLETE DECISION GUIDE, what is the priority order for checking graph algorithm signals?
options: Always start with the fastest algorithm (BFS) and escalate to slower ones

The decision guide checks in order: EULERIAN PATH first (most specific), then ORDERING/TOPO SORT, then MST, then INCREMENTAL/UNION-FIND, then ALL-PAIRS/FLOYD-WARSHALL, then K-HOP/BF, then NEGATIVE EDGES/BF, then WEIGHTED/DIJKSTRA, finally UNWEIGHTED/BFS or DFS; more specific signals (Eulerian path, MST) are checked before general ones (weighted, unweighted) to prevent misclassification
The order doesn't matter; all signals are checked simultaneously
The priority is: weighted first, then unweighted, then structural properties
theory_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's `selectGraphAlgorithm` function: the if-chain checks eulerianPath → ordering → mst → incremental → allPairs → kHop → negEdges → weighted → default BFS/DFS; this ordering ensures the most specific conditions (rare, distinctive signals like Eulerian path) are matched before general conditions (most problems are just 'weighted' or 'unweighted').

logic_mcq.question: How does Minimum Height Trees (#310) use Kahn's ALGORITHM structure, and what does it remove instead of in-degree-0 vertices?
options: Minimum Height Trees uses standard Kahn's for directed cycle detection

MHT uses ITERATIVE LEAF PRUNING — structurally identical to Kahn's but for UNDIRECTED trees: instead of removing zero-in-degree vertices (sources), it repeatedly removes LEAVES (vertices with degree 1 = only one connection); each pruning round removes all current leaves and creates new leaves from their former neighbours; when only 1 or 2 vertices remain (the centroid), those are the roots giving minimum height; 'remaining > 2' replaces Kahn's 'queue not empty' as the termination condition
MHT requires Bellman-Ford because tree heights are weighted
MHT uses DFS to find the longest path (diameter) and returns its midpoint
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's code: `while (remaining > 2)` removes leaves iteratively, analogous to Kahn's removing zero-in-degree vertices; the leaf (degree-1 node) in an undirected tree is the analog of a zero-in-degree vertex in a DAG; the centroid nodes that survive are the 1-2 vertices giving minimum height — the lesson explicitly calls this 'Kahn-style leaf pruning'.

syntax_mcq.question: In `findMinHeightTrees`, `const neighbour = [...adj[leaf]][0]` converts a Set to an array to access the single neighbour. Why does a leaf have exactly ONE element in its adjacency Set?
options: Leaves always have two neighbours; the second is the root

A LEAF in a tree has DEGREE 1 — exactly one edge connecting it to the rest of the tree; `adj[leaf].size === 1` is the leaf detection condition; since leaf's adjacency Set has exactly 1 element, spreading it `[...adj[leaf]]` creates a 1-element array and `[0]` accesses that single neighbour; after the leaf is removed (`adj[neighbour].delete(leaf)`), the former neighbour may become a new leaf if its degree drops to 1
Leaves have one element because adj is an array, not a Set
The spread is needed to handle leaves with multiple neighbours in special cases
syntax_mcq.explanation: A tree leaf has exactly degree 1 by definition; the condition `adj[i].size === 1` identifies leaves; spreading the size-1 Set and indexing [0] is the standard pattern for extracting the single element from a Set without iteration; the adjacent Set (not array) is used to enable O(1) deletion of bidirectional edges when a leaf is pruned.
